explanations.answer: He tears his clothes and puts on sackcloth
explanations.explanation: Mordecai, who raised Esther (Esther 2:7), tears his clothes and puts on sackcloth and ashes (Esther 4:1). In this chapter, that's what mourning looks like (Esther 4:3). He doesn't keep it quiet, either, because he goes out into the middle of the city. This man just got the worst news of his life, friend, and his clothes show it.

explanations.answer: He goes straight to Haman's house to argue
explanations.explanation: Haman is the king's top official (Esther 3:1), and the text never sends Mordecai to his door. Mordecai tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth and ashes, and goes out into the middle of the city (Esther 4:1). I think knocking on Haman's door would be a very short conversation anyway. Mordecai's grief goes out where the whole city can see it.

explanations.answer: He locks himself inside his home to hide
explanations.explanation: No hiding here, friend. The text says Mordecai goes out into the middle of the city, wailing loudly and bitterly (Esther 4:1). He tears his clothes and puts on sackcloth and ashes first. If you were looking for a quiet, private moment, this is the opposite of it.

explanations.answer: The law kept anyone in sackcloth out
explanations.explanation: Esther 4:2 says he went only as far as the king's gate, "because the law prohibited anyone wearing sackcloth from entering that gate." So Mordecai walks right up to the edge and stops. The sackcloth that shows his grief is the same thing that keeps him out. That's a rough spot to be stuck in, friend.

explanations.answer: The guards were under Haman's orders
explanations.explanation: The text gives a different reason, and it's a law. Esther 4:2 says the law prohibited anyone wearing sackcloth from entering that gate. It says nothing about the guards taking orders from Haman, the king's top official (Esther 3:1). So the sackcloth is what stops Mordecai at the gate.

explanations.answer: Esther had told him to wait right there
explanations.explanation: Esther hasn't even heard about Mordecai yet at this point. Her maidens and eunuchs tell her about him afterward (Esther 4:4). The reason for stopping is the law: no one wearing sackcloth could enter the king's gate (Esther 4:2). Mordecai just walked as far as the rules would let him.

Esther 4:3 says the Jews in every province "fasted, wept, and lamented, and many lay in sackcloth and ashes." Fasting means going without food, and that's how they mourn. News about the decree travels far, and so does the grief. It's a sad picture, friend, and I think we should let it be sad.

The text doesn't have the Jews picking up a fight here. Esther 4:3 says they fasted, wept, and lamented, and many lay in sackcloth and ashes. This is a whole people in mourning. Fasting is the word that fits the blank.

Nobody's running in this verse, friend. Esther 4:3 says there was great mourning among the Jews in every province, and that they fasted, wept, and lamented. Many lay in sackcloth and ashes. The word that fits is fasted.

explanations.answer: Clothes to wear instead of sackcloth
explanations.explanation: Esther 4:4 says the queen was overcome with distress and sent clothes for Mordecai to wear instead of his sackcloth. She sees her cousin in mourning and her first move is to get him something else to wear. That's a caring thing to do, friend. I think she wanted to help the only way she could from inside the palace.

explanations.answer: Silver to help him leave the city
explanations.explanation: There's no silver in this verse. Esther 4:4 says she sent clothes for Mordecai to wear instead of his sackcloth. She was overcome with distress when she heard about him. The gift was clothes.

explanations.answer: A message telling him to go home
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't have Esther sending that kind of message. Esther 4:4 says she sent clothes for Mordecai to wear instead of his sackcloth. She sends something he can hold, not just words. It's the clothes.
Not quite, friend. Esther 4:4 says she sent the clothes, "but he would not accept them." Mordecai stays in his sackcloth. That's one gift that goes right back.
That's right. Esther sent clothes for Mordecai to wear instead of his sackcloth, but he would not accept them (Esther 4:4). He stays in the sackcloth. The gift is returned, no receipt needed.

Yes, friend. Esther summoned Hathach, one of the king's eunuchs appointed to her. She sent him to Mordecai "to learn what was troubling him and why" (Esther 4:5). She doesn't know yet why her cousin is in sackcloth, so she sends someone to find out. Hathach is about to get a lot of steps in.

It's true, actually. Esther 4:5 says she summoned Hathach, one of the king's eunuchs appointed to her. She dispatched him to Mordecai to learn what was troubling him and why. Hathach goes out with a question and comes back with an answer.

explanations.answer: How much money Haman promised to pay
explanations.explanation: Esther 4:7 says Mordecai told Hathach all that had happened, including "the exact amount of money that Haman had promised to pay into the royal treasury in order to destroy the Jews." Haman is the king's top official (Esther 3:1). Mordecai has the exact figure. This man did his homework, friend.

explanations.answer: How many soldiers Haman would send
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention soldiers in this detail. Esther 4:7 says Mordecai told Hathach the exact amount of money Haman had promised to pay into the royal treasury. That's the number he knew. The detail was money, not soldiers.

explanations.answer: Who else helped Haman plan it all
explanations.explanation: No helpers are named in this verse. Esther 4:7 says Mordecai gave the exact amount of money that Haman had promised to pay into the royal treasury in order to destroy the Jews. That's the detail the text points out. Mordecai had the figure ready.

explanations.answer: A copy of the written decree
explanations.explanation: Esther 4:8 says Mordecai gave Hathach "a copy of the written decree issued in Susa for the destruction of the Jews," to show and explain to Esther. Words can get shaky when they're passed along, so he sends it in writing. Esther can see it for herself. That's smart, friend.

The ring was used to seal the decree (Esther 3:12), but it isn't what Mordecai hands over. Esther 4:8 says he gave Hathach a copy of the written decree issued in Susa. Hathach was to show and explain it to Esther. Mordecai sends the paper.

The text doesn't have a letter from Haman. Esther 4:8 says Mordecai gave Hathach a copy of the written decree issued in Susa for the destruction of the Jews. Hathach was to show and explain it to Esther. It's the decree itself.

Yes, friend. Esther 4:8 says Mordecai urged her "to approach the king, implore his favor, and plead before him for her people." He gives her the decree and the request together. It's a big ask, and he doesn't water it down.

It's true, actually. Mordecai sent Esther the decree and urged her to approach the king, implore his favor, and plead before him for her people (Esther 4:8). The request is right there in the verse. He asks for exactly that.

Esther says one law applies to every man or woman who approaches the king in the inner court without being summoned: "that he be put to death" (Esther 4:11). Only if the king extends the gold scepter may that person live. So walking in uninvited is a very risky move. That's the whole problem, friend.

explanations.answer: They are sent out of Susa
explanations.explanation: Being sent away isn't what the law says. Esther 4:11 says anyone who approaches the king in the inner court without being summoned is to be put to death. The only way out is if the king extends the gold scepter. The stakes are life and death.

Titles aren't the issue in this law. Esther 4:11 says the person who approaches the king in the inner court without being summoned is to be put to death. Only if the king extends the gold scepter may that person live. Esther isn't worried about her title.

explanations.answer: That the palace will keep her safe
explanations.explanation: Mordecai says, "Do not imagine that because you are in the king's palace you alone will escape the fate of all the Jews." (Esther 4:13) Esther has been living inside the palace walls. Mordecai tells her those walls won't save her. That's a tough thing to hear, friend.

explanations.answer: That the king will forget his decree
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't bring up the king forgetting anything. Mordecai tells Esther, "Do not imagine that because you are in the king's palace you alone will escape the fate of all the Jews." (Esther 4:13) His warning is about her own safety. It's the palace he's talking about.

explanations.answer: That Haman will change his mind
explanations.explanation: Haman, the king's top official (Esther 3:1), doesn't come up in Mordecai's warning. He says, "Do not imagine that because you are in the king's palace you alone will escape the fate of all the Jews." (Esther 4:13) The warning is about the palace not protecting her. That's the thing she's not to imagine.

Not quite, friend. Mordecai says that if she remains silent, "…relief and deliverance for the Jews will arise from another place, but you and your father's house will perish." (Esther 4:14) So he says help will come from another place. What he warns about is what happens to her and her family if she stays quiet.

That's right. Mordecai says, "…relief and deliverance for the Jews will arise from another place, but you and your father's house will perish." (Esther 4:14) He doesn't say there's no other hope. His warning is about what silence would cost Esther and her family.

Mordecai says that if she remains silent, relief for the Jews will arise from another place, "but you and your father's house will perish." (Esther 4:14) Perish is a strong word, and he picks it on purpose. I think Mordecai wants her to hear how serious this is. There's no sprinkles on that sentence, friend.
Wandering isn't what Mordecai warns about. Esther 4:14 says that if she remains silent, "you and your father's house will perish." Perish is the word in the verse. It's much heavier than wandering.

Hiding isn't in Mordecai's warning, friend. He says that if Esther remains silent, "you and your father's house will perish." (Esther 4:14) She was already inside the palace, and he tells her that won't save her. The word is perish.

explanations.answer: Maybe she became queen for this very moment
explanations.explanation: Mordecai asks, "And who knows if perhaps you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" (Esther 4:14) He asks it as a question and leaves it open. He's inviting Esther to think about why she is where she is. It's a question that makes you sit up, friend.

explanations.answer: Maybe the king never really trusted her
explanations.explanation: Mordecai says nothing about the king's trust. His question is, "And who knows if perhaps you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" (Esther 4:14) It's about Esther being in the kingdom at this time. That's what he asks her to think about.

explanations.answer: Maybe she was never meant to be queen
explanations.explanation: It's actually the opposite. Mordecai asks, "And who knows if perhaps you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" (Esther 4:14) He wonders whether her being there fits this very moment. He doesn't say she was never meant to be queen.

explanations.answer: Fast for her for three days
explanations.explanation: Esther says to assemble all the Jews who can be found in Susa and "fast for me. Do not eat or drink for three days, night or day." (Esther 4:16) That's no food and no drink for three days. It's a serious request, friend. She's asking the people to stand with her.

Standing at the gate isn't what she asks. Esther tells Mordecai to assemble the Jews in Susa and "fast for me. Do not eat or drink for three days, night or day." (Esther 4:16) Their part is to fast. It's a different kind of standing with her.

explanations.answer: Write a plea to the king
explanations.explanation: No letter-writing in this verse. Esther says to assemble all the Jews who can be found in Susa and "fast for me." (Esther 4:16) That means not eating or drinking for three days, night or day. The request is a fast.

Esther says, "I and my maidens will fast as you do." (Esther 4:16) She isn't asking the people to do something she won't do herself. Her maidens are in it with her. That's a queen who fasts right alongside everybody.
Scribes aren't mentioned in her plan. Esther says, "I and my maidens will fast as you do." (Esther 4:16) The ones fasting with her are her maidens. That's the word for the blank, friend.
The officials aren't in this verse. Esther says, "I and my maidens will fast as you do." (Esther 4:16) Her maidens fast with her. That's who fills the blank.

Yes, friend. Esther says, "After that, I will go to the king, even though it is against the law." (Esther 4:16) First comes the fast, then she goes. She knows what the law says about going uninvited (Esther 4:11), and she says it anyway.

It's true, actually. Esther says, "After that, I will go to the king, even though it is against the law." (Esther 4:16) She has already told Mordecai about the law (Esther 4:11), so she knows exactly what she's saying. She says she will go.
Yes, friend. Esther 4:17 says, "So Mordecai went and did all that Esther had instructed him." Earlier it was Mordecai giving the instructions. Now Esther gives them, and he follows them.

It's true, actually. Esther 4:17 says Mordecai "went and did all that Esther had instructed him." Esther was the one giving instructions here, and Mordecai did what she said. The verse doesn't leave anything out.
